newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-RICE, JORDAN SHINE IN EAST VICTORY AT ALL-STAR GAME.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-RICE, JORDAN SHINE IN EAST VICTORY AT ALL-STAR GAME.

text.p: Watched by the greatest players in NBA history, Glen Rice and Michael Jordan wrote a little history themselves in the Eastern Conference's 132-120 victory over the West at the 47th annual All-Star Game Sunday.
Rice, the Most Valuable Player, scored an All-Star record 20 points in the third quarter and Jordan recorded the first triple-double in All-Star Game history.

On a day when 47 of the 50 greatest players in league history stood before the fans at halftime, Rice shot his way to the greatest quarter and Jordan posted the greatest all-around game in the history of the series, which the East leads 30-17.
"Obviously I'm the best player in the world today, I'm the MVP," Rice joked. "But it's not going to go to my head.
"Most of our guys were in awe of the 50 players. We watched on TV at the half. I will never forget doing it in front of these guys I admired and tried to follow and emulate."

"I was in awe of the 50 great players," said Jordan. "I sat down and talked to Bill Russell, trying to educate myself as to a lot of things about the NBA. I asked Wilt Chamberlain if he was tired the night he got the 100 points, and he said he was.
"This was an unbelievable experience just playing in front of them, let alone getting the triple double."
Eastern coach Doug Collins of the Detroit Pistons said he tried to help Rice and Jordan achieve their records.
"We made a conscious effort to put Rice back in so he could get his record, and we told Michael about the rebounds and he went out there to get nothing else."
Both coaches raved like starstruck fans about the day.
"This was the greatest experience of my life as a coach," said the West's Rudy Tomjanovich, who skippered the Houston Rockets to two NBA championships.
"Everyone in our room was in awe of all the great players, some of whom I played against and some of whom are only legends to me when I was a kid."

"Coaching this was one of the most humbling experiences of my life," said Collins. "Being out there with the super athletes on my team and watching them watch the 50 greatest at the half made this a great event."
The East took control for good in the third quarter behind Rice, who shot poorly in Saturday's Long Distance Shootout and missed six of seven first-half shots.

The Charlotte Hornets guard drilled four straight three-pointers and never cooled off, making 8-of-11 shots in the period as the East built a 97-87 bulge. He had more points in the period than any other player had in the game.
Rice broke the record set in 1968 by Philadelphia 76ers guard Hal Greer, on hand as one of the 50 greatest players. Rice ended up with 26 points, including a record 24 in the second half.
Chamberlain -- also a top-50 member -- scored 23 points in a half in 1962. Tom Chambers matched it in 1987.

Jordan, the first of the 50 introduced at intermission, keyed a second-quarter surge that saw the East erase almost all of a 23-point deficit in a five-minute span. The superstar guard of the Chicago Bulls did not shoot well but finished with 14 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists.

"I wasn't in synch," said Jordan. "I wasn't hitting my shots. The assists you expect but the rebounds are really something different. It was really unbelievable. Do you know how many triple doubles Oscar Robertson has? And he never did it in an All-Star Game.

Orlando Magic point guard Penny Hardaway made sure the West didn't rally, directing the offence and finishing with 19 points. Milwaukee Bucks forward Vin Baker added 19 for the East, which has won three of the last four All-Star Games.

Guards Latrell Sprewell of the Golden State Warriors and Gary Payton of the Seattle Supersonics led the West with 19 and 17 points, respectively. All 24 players scored and both teams reached 120 points in a regulation game for the first time since 1989.

"Playing in a wide-open game like this fits my style," said Sprewell. "The guys are not playing much defence. They're trying not to get hurt and they want to have fun, and that's what basketball's all about."
"We lost because the All-Star Game is like playground ball, and they played a little defence and we didn't," said Payton.

After a half-season of watching the plodding Cleveland Cavaliers, fans at Gund Arena were treated to a track meet speeded up by the absence due to injury of bigmen Patrick Ewing and Alonzo Mourning on the East and Shaquille O'Neal for the West.
Houston's Charles Barkley and Clyde Drexler also sat out with ailments as the game featured six first-time All-Stars.
Of the 50 great players named by the NBA, only three could not attend.
Pete Maravich has died.
Jerry West, the guard once known as "Mr. Clutch" and now mastermind of the Los Angeles Lakers, was absent for medical reasons.
The announcement of the absent O'Neal, the Lakers centre who was a controversial choice as an all-time great in just his fifth season, was booed during the halftime ceremonies.
